guideTitle: 5 Best 5G Cell Phone Signal Boosters for Home (2026)
metaTitle: Best 5G Cell Signal Boosters for Home (2026)
metaDescription: Five 5G cell phone signal boosters for home compared by coverage claims, antennas and install effort, to fix weak signal in bedrooms, offices and living areas.
mainKeyword: best 5g cell phone signal boosters for home
introParagraphs: A home booster takes a weak outdoor signal, amplifies it and rebroadcasts it indoors, which is why coverage claims are only half the story. The five kits here advertise anything from a 2,500 square foot HiBoost with 62dB gain to the Hiboost 15K 2.0 covering up to 12,000 square feet, with two indoor antennas.

Our top pick is that Hiboost 15K 2.0 because it pairs the largest coverage claim with two indoor panel antennas for bigger or two-story layouts. The YJXcell at 8,000 square feet and the subroad at 5,000 square feet sit in the middle, while the HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit is the choice for two or three rooms. The BoostHome is the lowest-cost pick and the only one whose listing disagrees with itself on coverage.

We evaluated each pick on published specs and buyer feedback, not on hands-on installs, and we treat every square footage number as a best case. Real results depend on the outdoor signal where the antenna sits, the construction of your house and how far apart the antennas are placed.

products.name: Hiboost 15K 2.0 Home Booster
products.description:
The Hiboost 15K 2.0 is the largest kit in this guide, advertising coverage of up to 12,000 square feet with two included indoor panel antennas. Having two antennas lets you serve two zones, such as a main floor and an upstairs office, from one booster. It supports 5G and 4G LTE signals for major carriers including Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile.

The listing talks up premium materials and thicker outdoor cabling, which matters because a long cable run is part of any big install. The trade is price: it is the highest-cost pick here, and the install is busier than a single-antenna kit. The 12,000 square foot figure is a ceiling, not a promise, since coverage still depends on the signal your outdoor antenna captures.

Plan the install carefully, with the outdoor antenna high and well separated from the indoor ones to avoid feedback. Against the YJXcell, which also uses two inside antennas but claims 8,000 square feet, this is the pick for a larger or multi-level home. If you only need a couple of rooms, the 2,500 square foot HiBoost is a more sensible fit.

products.description:
The YJXcell Home Office Booster advertises coverage of 8,000 square feet and up, with two inside antennas included. That makes it the budget route to a big-home setup, at a lower-middle price tier. The listing is upfront about reality: with only one or two bars outside, the indoor area drops to about 600 square feet.

That honesty is useful, because it shows how much the outdoor signal drives the result. If your phone already gets decent signal at the roof or window where the outdoor antenna goes, you should see far more coverage. If outdoor signal is weak, expect much less than the headline number.

Install is busier with two antennas, so plan a cable route and keep the inside units away from the outdoor one. Compared with the Hiboost 15K 2.0, it gives up the biggest coverage claim for a lower cost. Against the subroad at 5,000 square feet, it adds a second inside antenna and a bigger headline figure.

products.name: subroad Home Cell Repeater, Up to 5,000 Sq Ft
products.description:
The subroad Home Cell Repeater claims coverage up to 5,000 square feet and lists support for 5G, 4G LTE, 3G and 2G signals. It works with phones, hotspots, tablets and laptops from all US and Canadian carriers, which is handy if your household mixes devices. Mid-range pricing puts it between the budget BoostHome and the larger kits.

The listing focuses on solving dropped calls, buffering and undelivered messages, which are the problems most homeowners notice first. What it does not give is a gain figure, so you cannot compare raw amplification with the 62dB HiBoost. Because 5,000 square feet is a maximum, a typical single-story home with a decent outdoor signal is the realistic target.

Ownership is straightforward: outdoor antenna, cable, booster and one inside antenna. Compared with the YJXcell, it uses one inside antenna instead of two, so it suits a simpler layout. Next to the HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit, it nearly doubles the claimed area for a similar price tier.

products.name: HiBoost Home Office Booster, Up to 2,500 Sq Ft
products.description:
The HiBoost 2,500 square foot booster targets two to three rooms, such as a bedroom, living area or small office. It lists 62dB gain and automatic gain adjustment, and you can check signal strength through an app or the main unit display. The listing says it can lift a signal from one bar to three or four bars, which is a realistic goal for a small area.

Automatic gain control protects the network by adjusting the booster to the incoming signal, so you do not need to tune it yourself. The downside is the smallest coverage claim of the kits and a high price for the area it serves. If your whole home is under 2,500 square feet, though, the app guidance is a plus.

It is a good choice for first-time buyers who want to see what the booster is doing. Compared with the subroad at 5,000 square feet, it covers less but gives clearer feedback. Against the Hiboost 15K 2.0, it is much simpler to set up, with one indoor antenna and fewer cable runs.

The BoostHome Multiroom Cell Booster is the lowest-cost kit here, aimed at 5G and 4G LTE for all US carriers. Its listing is inconsistent: the title says up to 8,000 square feet while the feature text says one to two rooms and up to 5,000 square feet. That mismatch is a warning to treat any coverage number with care.

The more useful detail is the weak signal note, which says one or two bars outside gives roughly 800 square feet inside. That is the number to plan around, and it is realistic for one or two rooms. For a renter or first-time buyer trying to solve a single bedroom, the low price makes sense.

The install is light, with a single indoor antenna, but you must still place the antennas apart. Compared with the YJXcell, it costs less but gives a smaller practical area. Against the HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit, it has no app or display for checking performance.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A booster only amplifies the signal it can capture at the outdoor antenna. The YJXcell listing says one or two bars outside gives roughly 600 square feet of indoor coverage, while the BoostHome says about 800. Test your outdoor signal at the roof or window, using a mapping app or a signal reading on your phone. If you cannot find a spot with at least some signal, no kit from the Hiboost 15K 2.0 to the BoostHome will help.

Coverage depends on floor plan, construction materials and the outdoor signal, so no maker can guarantee a square footage figure. The Hiboost 15K 2.0 claims up to 12,000 square feet, but that is a best-case number. The BoostHome listing even disagrees with itself between 8,000 and 5,000 square feet. Choose a kit one step larger than your home if your signal is weak.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Gain and the kit you actually need
buyingCriteria.explanation: Gain tells you how much a booster amplifies, and the HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit lists 62dB. Sources differ on typical figures, with one weBoost-linked source citing +65dB for home kits and another citing 63 to 72dB for broadband boosters. With a weak outdoor signal, gain matters most, while with a strong signal, output power matters more. Do not treat any single gain figure as a hard standard.

If the outside and inside antennas are too close, the booster can feed back on itself, lowering gain or shutting off. Required distance is model specific, with weBoost suggesting about 25 to 30 feet vertical and SureCall listing about 60 feet for one model. Two-antenna kits like the Hiboost 15K 2.0 and YJXcell make this planning more important. A forced lower gain shrinks the coverage area, so respect the manual.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Number of rooms and indoor antennas
buyingCriteria.explanation: The HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit targets two to three rooms, while the Hiboost 15K 2.0 and YJXcell include two indoor antennas for larger layouts. One antenna serves one zone well, but a long or two-story house may need two. Place the indoor antenna in the room where you most use your phone. If you work upstairs and sleep downstairs, a two-antenna kit is more useful.

Check that the booster supports the bands your carrier uses and that it carries an FCC ID and network protection wording. The subroad lists 5G, 4G LTE, 3G and 2G, while the HiBoost kits list all major carriers. Many 5G signals ride on existing 4G bands, so the 5G label alone does not tell you much. Confirm your phone's bands in field test mode before choosing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Coverage claims and honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the published coverage numbers and how realistically each listing frames them. The YJXcell and BoostHome both publish weak-signal figures of roughly 600 and 800 square feet, which scored well for transparency. The BoostHome loses points for disagreeing with itself between 8,000 and 5,000 square feet. The Hiboost 15K 2.0 has the largest claim.

howWeEvaluated.title: Gain and signal control
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at listed gain and automatic gain control. The HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit lists 62dB with AGC and an app, while the subroad gives no gain figure. Picks that explain gain control scored higher. Gain figures are seller claims and vary by source.

howWeEvaluated.title: Antennas and layout flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: Two-antenna kits like the Hiboost 15K 2.0 and YJXcell scored best for large or multi-level homes. Single-antenna kits like the subroad and BoostHome suit simpler layouts. We also looked at cable quality, where the Hiboost lists thicker outdoor cabling. The strongest pick for flexibility is the 15K, and the most basic is the BoostHome.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of setup
howWeEvaluated.description: We reviewed how clearly each listing explains installation and monitoring. The HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit offers an app or display for checking signal strength, which makes tuning easier. Two-antenna kits need more planning. Beginners should favor kits with feedback.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value for the home size
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared relative price against the area each kit realistically serves. The BoostHome is the lowest-cost pick, while the Hiboost 15K 2.0 is the highest. The YJXcell offers the most coverage claim per dollar in the mid-range. Value is highest when the kit matches the home size.

faq.q: How do I choose between these home boosters?
faq.a: Start with home size and layout. The HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit suits two to three rooms, the subroad suits an average house, and the Hiboost 15K 2.0 and YJXcell suit larger homes with two antennas. Then check your outdoor signal, because it limits every kit.

faq.q: Why is my coverage smaller than the box says?
faq.a: Coverage claims are best-case numbers based on a strong outdoor signal. The YJXcell says one or two bars outside gives roughly 600 square feet, and the BoostHome says about 800. Walls, floors and construction materials also reduce reach.
Only where the 5G signal rides on bands the booster supports. Many 5G signals use existing 4G bands, so band compatibility matters more than the label. Check your phone's bands before buying.

faq.q: Why do the antennas need to be separated?
faq.a: If the inside and outside antennas are too close, the booster can pick up its own output and feed back. It then lowers gain, and if that fails it must shut off. Required distance varies by model, so follow the manual.

faq.q: Is a more expensive booster always better?
faq.a: No. The Hiboost 15K 2.0 costs the most because it covers the most, but a small home gains nothing from it. The HiBoost 2,500 square foot kit fits a small home better. Match the kit to the area.

faq.q: Do I need to tell my carrier I installed a booster?
faq.a: Registration rules vary, and none of the five listings here spells out a carrier registration requirement. Check the product page and your carrier's policy before installing. Look for an FCC ID and network protection wording as a basic safety check.
